lineas.texto: In an open pot, water can't get hotter than 100 degrees Celsius. No matter how big the fire.
Extra heat just turns more water into steam, and the steam floats away.
A pressure cooker traps that steam.
A rubber ring seals the lid, so the steam has nowhere to go.
The steam piles up and presses down on the water.
And water under pressure can't boil until it reaches about 120 degrees.
Twenty degrees hotter cooks food two or three times faster.
Too much pressure? A little weight on top lifts up and lets steam hiss out.
That's the hiss you hear in the kitchen. What should we explain next?
